children: By Fabiana Negrin Ochoa
Alex Zhavoronkov, founder and co-chief executive of techbio company Insilico, is among the scientists who have devoted countless hours to studying aging.
He has a reality-check for anyone who thinks that artificial intelligence means that the ability to double lifespans is tantalizingly close.
"Absolute nonsense," said Zhavoronkov, whose company uses AI to discover and develop drugs.
In 150 years of discovery, no drug has been clinically proven to extend life, he said in an interview. "Regardless of how rich you are...you cannot buy one year of life with a drug."
What could be within reach in the next decade or so--in the most optimistic scenario--is the ability to dial back a person's biological clock, said Zhavoronkov.
In a study published in Nature Biotechnology, researchers evaluated Insilico's investigational drug--known as rentosertib--for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, an age-related lung disease.

They used six independently developed proteomic aging clocks--machine-learning algorithms that analyze hundreds to thousands of proteins to establish a person's biological age. Whereas chronological age measures years, biological age assesses the health of cells and organs to predict lifespan and risk of disease.
The clocks consistently indicated declines in the biological ages of rentosertib-treated patients. Zhavoronkov, who co-authored the paper, said the most significant reduction was six years.
"Six years is very promising, right? But I can tell you that it will take us a decade to prove that it's anti-aging--if it gets approved," he said.
A preliminary trial on a small group of patients--known as Phase 2a--of rentosertib for IPF concluded last year. It is now in Phase 3, the final stage before a drug gets approval to hit the market.

Zhavoronkov said the research by Insilico and scientists from institutions including Harvard, Peking University and Westlake University is the first clinical evaluation of an AI-driven innovative drug candidate in aging research.
Success in further, larger trials would give support to the AI-driven model that Insilico and other biotech firms are pioneering.

Insilico's approach is to tackle aging and disease simultaneously. It says this strategy makes clinical trials more commercially viable than the traditional route of trying to repurpose generics for anti-aging.

"Our AI is tailored to capture the dual-purpose drugs that are working in aging and disease," Zhavoronkov said. "Our core objective...is to solve aging in order to give you time to solve everything else."
Zhavoronkov said rentosertib has shown promising results in improving lung function and biological age, with the latter effect observable in the brain and other organs.

Asked what it means to shave years off a person's brain age, he said: "The right answer is we don't know." The only way to check that would be via a longitudinal study spanning 10 years or so, he added.
Confirmation of rentosertib's age-reversing potential requires further investigation, including on non-IPF patients.

AI can give drugmakers some "superpowers," Zhavoronkov said, but they must establish clinical significance and safety. Even with an AI-accelerated timeline, that will take at least a decade, the Insilico founder said.
"We want more scientists to experiment," he said.

Since Insilico published Phase 2a results in Nature Medicine last June, several groups have started working on the same drug in the context of heart fibrosis, obesity and other indications, he said, "with some very promising results I cannot talk about yet."
For now, the main focus will be on the ongoing Phase 3 trial of rentosertib to treat IPF.
At this stage there is still a roughly 30% probability of failure, Zhavoronkov said.
Success would be the strongest clinical validation yet of Insilico's Pharma.AI platform, Citi analysts said in a recent note.

Highlighting rentosertib as Insilico's biggest valuation catalyst, Citi said it is bullish on the company's ability to commercialize AI drugs, noting its string of multibillion-dollar licensing deals with the likes of Eli Lilly.
But it also flagged significant risks. Phase 2a provides limited evidence on chronic exposure, and longer treatment could reveal safety or tolerability limitations, Citi said.

An inability to replicate Phase 2a efficacy signals would reduce rentosertib's value, and even if efficacy is demonstrated, safety-driven dose modification could constrain commercial uptake, the analysts said.
Insilico has plenty of other promising assets, but revenue and profitability are difficult to forecast given the dependence on deals transactions and milestone timing, they added.
Even if Phase 3 fails, Zhavoronkov says the research has still created something valuable: a template for how to discover anti-aging therapeutics more quickly and efficiently.
He acknowledges the challenges ahead, but if rentosertib delivers on his most ambitious hopes, he sees a scenario where it could one day be as accessible as Tylenol.
"This drug can be made very cheap because it's a small molecule, right? It can be aspirin," he said. "That's a trillion-dollar opportunity."
Jiahui Huang contributed to this report
